articles.title: The Global Story - Is the world giving up on the US dollar? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Economist Kenneth Rogoff argues that that the era of dollar dominance may be ending
articles.body:
World Service , · 02 Sep 2026 , · 27 mins

America’s national debt recently hit a new milestone of $40 trillion. It is estimated that interest payments on the national debt are now the second largest expense in the US government budget, trailing only social security. How was the US able to borrow so much and for so long? One answer, according Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff, is the US dollar’s status as the world’s reserve currency. In this episode, Rogoff, former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, explains how the US dollar came to enjoy this hegemonic status, what being the world’s reserve currency actually means in practice, and why he believes the dollar is now in decline. articles.summary: And, why did Justin call Donald Trump from a train?
articles.body: Americanswers is back for a bank holiday special and this week we're answering the questions you've always wanted to ask on American politics! For example, Zohran Mamdani can't run for president of the United States as he was born in Uganda, but could he take up a cabinet position in a future Democrat administration? Is there a precedent for such a move, and would he even want it? Another Americaster wants to know if we see any similarities between Donald Trump and former president Lyndon B. Johnson. LBJ grew up in Anthony's home state of Texas and, unlike Trump, rose to the presidency after positions in Congress and two years as vice president. Despite the obvious differences, both men were considered outsiders in American politics. Do they share anything else in common? Plus, is money still as important as ever when running for president? The Democratic Party is being outspent by Republicans ahead of the midterm elections but that doesn't mean the candidates themselves are strapped for cash. Has social media changed the game when it comes to political campaigning? articles.title: The Interview - Daron Acemoglu, Economist: Liberal democracy is in crisis - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Economist Daron Acemoglu on liberal democracy in crisis and how AI could make it worse
articles.body:
World Service , · 02 Sep 2026 , · 22 mins

BBC Newsnight presenter Paddy O’Connell speaks to Nobel Prize-winning economist Daron Acemoglu about why he thinks liberal democracy is in crisis, and how artificial intelligence could make it worse. Daron argues that liberal democracy worked because people were given a say in how they were governed and then benefited from their country’s economy as it prospered. But western governments have made major decisions on issues like immigration without first building public agreement, something which was once important. In an interview with BBC Newsnight, he says that together, these changes have left many working people feeling that politicians no longer listen to them and have helped to fuel a rise in populism. Now Daron warns that the way artificial intelligence is developed and used, so far without consensus, could make it worse, by widening inequality and putting people out of work. “AI is going to transform every aspect of our lives, and we're not being asked. We have no say in how AI is going to shape our society. I mean people in the UK, people in the US. Even worse for 6 billion people who are outside of the US, UK, China. Their lives are going to be completely reshaped by AI and they have zero say whatsoever,” he says. The Interview brings you conversations with people shaping our world, from all over the world. The best interviews from the BBC, including episodes with Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk, South African minister Gayton McKenzie and New York Times White House correspondent Maggie Haberman. articles.title: Trump sugere renomear Estreito de Ormuz para 'Estreito de Trump' | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova declaração ocorre em meio à retomada dos ataques entre EUA e Irã e à disputa por uma das principais rotas do petróleo mundial.
articles.summary: Nova declaração ocorre em meio à retomada dos ataques entre EUA e Irã e à disputa por uma das principais rotas do petróleo mundial.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , sugeriu nesta quarta-feira (2) renomear o Estreito de Ormuz para "Estreito de Trump" , em meio à disputa com o Irã pela via navegável estratégica.

"Agora que o temos sob controle dos EUA, deveríamos mudar o nome do Estreito de Ormuz para ESTREITO DE TRUMP???", questionou Trump em sua plataforma Truth Social.

A declaração acontece em meio a retomada das trocas de ataques entre os dois países. Na manhã desta quarta, o país persa culpou os americanos por um ataque a uma festa de casamento que ocorria em Kuhestak, no sul do Irã, em meio a uma nova ofensiva . Segundo a Cruz Vermelha, quatro pessoas morreram e 50 ficaram feridas. Teerã prometeu retaliação. Os EUA negaram .

🔎 O Estreito de Ormuz fica entre o Irã e a Península Arábica, conecta o Golfo Pérsico ao Golfo de Omã e é considerado uma das principais artérias do comércio global de petróleo. Cerca de 20% do petróleo consumido no mundo passa pela região.

Não é a primeira vez que Trump afirma que o Estreito de Ormuz pertence aos Estados Unidos. Em 14 de agosto, o republicano afirmou que pretendia declarar o Estreito de Ormuz como território dos EUA , ampliando a pressão sobre Teerã em meio às negociações para encerrar o conflito.

O governo iraniano reagiu dizendo que a passagem está sob sua autoridade e que não se deixaria intimidar pelas ameaças americanas.

Quatro dias depois, Trump voltou a provocar o Irã ao compartilhar uma montagem que identificava Ormuz como "novo território dos EUA" . A imagem foi publicada nos perfis oficiais do presidente e da Casa Branca. Em resposta, o vice-ministro das Relações Exteriores do Irã, Kazem Gharibabadi , afirmou que a "ilusão" de Trump sobre o estreito seria corrigida.

Trump fala com a imprensa na Casa Branca após assinar ordem executiva renomeando o Lago Ontário como Lago América — Foto: Evan Vucci/Reuters

articles.title: Governo do RJ abre ao público dados de compras, contratos e viagens em Portal da Transparência | G1
articles.standfirst: Ricardo Couto de Castro apresentou, nesta quarta-feira (2), o programa Gestão em Números. Entre os dados que podem ser consultados estão gastos com combustível de veículos oficiais e passagens aéreas.
articles.summary: Ricardo Couto de Castro apresentou, nesta quarta-feira (2), o programa Gestão em Números. Entre os dados que podem ser consultados estão gastos com combustível de veículos oficiais e passagens aéreas.
articles.body:
O Governo do Estado do Rio de Janeiro apresentou, nesta quarta-feira (2), o programa “Gestão em Números”, que reúne dados sobre receitas e despesas da administração estadual. Durante a coletiva, o governador em exercício, Ricardo Couto, anunciou uma nova versão do Portal da Transparência, com mais informações sobre compras, contratos e gastos do governo.

O Portal da Transparência já permitia consultar informações como salários de servidores e despesas públicas. A ferramenta agora amplia a quantidade de dados disponíveis e facilita o cruzamento das informações pela população.

Entre os dados que podem ser consultados estão os gastos com combustível de veículos oficiais. É possível verificar quanto cada órgão do governo estadual pagou e relacionar as despesas aos veículos utilizados.

O portal também reúne informações sobre passagens aéreas compradas para autoridades, assessores e servidores públicos. Os dados podem ser consultados em tabelas e mapas disponibilizados na plataforma.

Segundo o secretário de Planejamento, Rafael Ventura Abreu, as informações serão atualizadas mensalmente pelos servidores responsáveis. O governo também informou que os dados disponíveis desde 2024 passarão por atualização ao longo dos próximos meses.

Governo do RJ apresenta portal que permite consultar gastos públicos e cruzar dados — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A ferramenta permite que o cidadão acompanhe os gastos públicos e identifique possíveis inconsistências. Caso encontre alguma irregularidade ou queira obter informações adicionais, o cidadão pode procurar a secretaria responsável ou fazer um pedido pela Lei de Acesso à Informação (LAI).

A proposta do governo é ampliar o acesso aos dados públicos e facilitar o acompanhamento, pela população, de como os recursos estaduais são utilizados.

articles.title: Incêndio em lixão em Lábrea dura um mês e cobre cidade de fumaça | G1
articles.standfirst: Lixão fica a cerca de 1 quilômetro da área urbana e a aproximadamente 800 metros do Hospital Geral de Lábrea. De acordo com o morador, a fumaça tem alcançado diferentes regiões da cidade.
articles.summary: Incêndio em lixão em Lábrea é investigado como criminoso após fumaça atingir hospital e cobrir a cidade por mais de 30 dias consecutivos.
articles.body:
Lábrea , no sul do Amazonas, amanheceu coberta por fumaça nesta quarta-feira (2) por causa de um incêndio no lixão da cidade. Segundo um morador ouvido pelo g1 , que trabalha próximo ao local, as chamas atingem a área há mais de 30 dias.

O lixão fica a cerca de 1 quilômetro da área urbana e a aproximadamente 800 metros do Hospital Geral de Lábrea. De acordo com o morador, a fumaça tem alcançado diferentes regiões da cidade.

Ele relatou que equipes do Corpo de Bombeiros do Amazonas (CBMAM) já atuaram no local em outras ocasiões, principalmente quando o fogo se intensifica. No entanto, afirma que as chamas voltam a surgir após os trabalhos de combate.

"Os bombeiros atuam no local quando o fogo está muito intenso. Já foram lá algumas vezes, porém não eliminam as chamas completamente e volta a reacender", relatou.

Ao g1 , o secretário municipal de Meio Ambiente, Zerisfran Teixeira, informou que o incêndio estava controlado na manhã desta quarta-feira, mas que as equipes permaneciam no local.

Segundo ele, a prefeitura trata o caso como um incêndio criminoso e comunicou a ocorrência à polícia.

"O fogo está controlado. Foi um incêndio criminoso, mas ninguém sabe quem tocou fogo. Estamos investigando para saber quem foi e comunicamos à polícia", afirmou.

O secretário disse ainda que o lixão é cercado e que a prefeitura reforçou o controle de acesso ao local com vigilantes nas duas entradas, durante o dia e a noite. "Nós temos vigias nas duas entradas para que não entre mais ninguém no lixão. Agora tem vigia 24 horas", disse.

Conforme a prefeitura, o combate ao incêndio ocorre com apoio das secretarias municipais de Meio Ambiente e Infraestrutura, do Corpo de Bombeiros e do Prevfogo. Máquinas também são usadas para revirar os resíduos e ajudar no controle das chamas.

"Nós estamos trabalhando em quatro frentes aqui para combater esse incêndio. Estamos em parceria com a Secretaria de Infraestrutura, com as máquinas, com o Corpo de Bombeiros, com o Prevfogo e com a Secretaria de Meio Ambiente", explicou.

Apesar de afirmar que a situação está controlada, Zerisfran destacou que incêndios em lixões são difíceis de combater e que não há previsão para o encerramento dos trabalhos.

"Fogo em lixão não é tão fácil de ser combatido. Nós estamos aqui, mas não temos hora para sair", afirmou.

O secretário informou que a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente monitora diariamente a qualidade do ar em Lábrea. Segundo ele, quando os índices apresentam piora, a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde é acionada para orientar a população.

"Nós temos um aparelho aqui na Secretaria que mede a qualidade do ar e, todos os dias, divulgamos. Quando o ar não está legal, comunicamos a Secretaria de Saúde, que faz as orientações para a população", explicou.

Lábrea fica encoberta por fumaça após incêndio em lixão — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Zerisfran informou ainda que a prefeitura trabalha para desativar o lixão atual e implantar um aterro sanitário no município. Segundo ele, o terreno já foi aprovado e a documentação necessária está em fase de encaminhamento.

"Vamos transferir esse lixão e fazer o nosso aterro sanitário. Já está tudo encaminhado. O terreno já foi aprovado e estamos passando a documentação para dar entrada no aterro sanitário", afirmou.

O combate ao incêndio continua nesta quarta-feira, segundo a prefeitura. A administração municipal informou que acompanha a ocorrência em conjunto com os órgãos envolvidos.

articles.title: Risco de incêndio: Jeep faz recall no Brasil deWrangler e Gladiator | G1
articles.standfirst: Possível defeito no circuito elétrico da bomba de direção pode provocar princípio de incêndio. Campanha no Brasil atinge 1.472 unidades; tempo de inspeção e reparo é de 30 minutos.
articles.summary: Possível defeito no circuito elétrico da bomba de direção pode provocar princípio de incêndio. Campanha no Brasil atinge 1.472 unidades; tempo de inspeção e reparo é de 30 minutos.
articles.body:
Jeep Wrangler Rubicon 2025 — Foto: Divulgação / Stellantis

A Stellantis, dona da marca Jeep , anunciou um recall no Brasil dos modelos Gladiator Rubicon (modelo 2022 a 2025) e Wrangler (anos-modelo 2021 a 2025) por risco de incêndio.

O chamado envolve 1.472 unidades dos dois modelos e é motivado por uma falha identificada no circuito elétrico da bomba de direção eletro-hidráulica dos veículos .

Em situações extremas, segundo a marca, esse defeito de funcionamento pode provocar um princípio de incêndio .

De acordo com o comunicado da Stellantis, isso traz riscos de danos materiais e lesões físicas aos ocupantes e terceiros.

Para solucionar o problema, a montadora orienta os proprietários dos modelos afetados a agendarem o atendimento na rede de concessionárias da marca.

O procedimento consiste em uma verificação técnica do sistema e no reparo do componente, com um tempo estimado de execução de aproximadamente 30 minutos.

Os números dos chassis envolvidos na campanha são:

Jeep Gladiator Rubicon 2025 — Foto: Divulgação / Stellantis

Segundo comunicado da empresa, " foi identificada a possibilidade de falha na fixação dos cintos de segurança do banco traseiro, que pode, eventualmente, ocasionar a falta de retenção dos ocupantes do veículo em caso de frenagem brusca ou acidente, consequentemente, potencializando a ocorrência de danos materiais, físicos ou até mesmo fatais ".

A orientação aos proprietários das 5.810 unidades envolvidas no recall é entrar em contato com uma concessionária RAM e agendar a verificação.

Se necessário, será feita a fixação correta dos cintos de segurança para o banco traseiro.

Segundo a Stellantis, os serviços de inspeção e eventual reparo são gratuitos e levam 30 minutos para serem concluídos.

RAM 1500 — Foto: Divulgação / Stellantis

A agência Reuters noticiou em julho que a Stellantis, dona da marca RAM, faria um recall de mais de 1,5 milhão de unidades da picape 1500 por problemas nos cintos de segurança .

Os modelos envolvidos na campanha foram fabricados entre 2019 e 2026 . São 1,27 milhão de picapes nos Estados Unidos, 156 mil no Canadá, 15 mil no México e cerca de 75 mil fora da América do Norte.

O defeito detectado nos EUA, o mesmo das picapes vendidas no Brasil, está nos pontos de ancoragem dos cintos de segurança na segunda fileira de assentos, especificamente nas fivelas do cinto do meio e do cinto do passageiro que vai à esquerda, logo atrás do motorista.

De acordo com o informado pela agência Reuters em julho, “o problema pode afetar o desempenho do sistema de cintos de segurança da segunda fileira de bancos e aumentar o risco de ferimentos aos ocupantes. A Stellantis tem conhecimento de um caso de lesão possivelmente relacionado ao defeito que motivou o recall, mas não há registro de mortes”.

articles.title: Empreendedorismo movimenta Uberlândia e impulsiona desenvolvimento da cidade  | G1
articles.standfirst: Crescimento de negócios em diferentes setores revela força, a energia e o potencial para continuar avançando
articles.summary: Crescimento de negócios em diferentes setores revela força, a energia e o potencial para continuar avançando
articles.body:
Novos negócios fomentam crescimento econômico — Foto: Secretaria de Governo e Comunicação/PMU

Uberlândia vive um momento de transformação marcado pela força e pela energia de quem empreende, investe e acredita no potencial da cidade. Em diferentes setores da economia, novos negócios surgem, empresas ampliam suas operações e empreendedores encontram espaço para transformar ideias em oportunidades.

Mais do que movimentar o comércio e gerar renda, esse ambiente empreendedor contribui para criar empregos, estimular a inovação e fortalecer uma cadeia econômica que beneficia toda a população.

Fabio Emanoel, Diretor comercial no segmento de combustíveis — Foto: Acervo pessoal

Na avaliação de Fabio Emanoel, diretor comercial em distribuidora de combustíveis, Uberlândia tem uma característica muito forte: é uma cidade que não para de empreender, crescer e buscar novas oportunidades.

“Esse movimento é um verdadeiro combustível para o desenvolvimento da cidade. Acreditamos nesse potencial e, por isso, seguimos investindo e ampliando nossa presença na cidade, promovendo o crescimento dos negócios e contribuindo ativamente para que Uberlândia continue avançando”, destaca.

Em Uberlândia, o empreendedorismo faz parte da dinâmica de uma das principais cidades de Minas Gerais. Pequenos negócios, empresas de médio porte e grandes empreendimentos convivem em um ecossistema que amplia as possibilidades de crescimento econômico.

Cada nova empresa representa mais do que uma atividade comercial. É também a criação de postos de trabalho, a contratação de fornecedores, a circulação de recursos e o surgimento de novos serviços para atender às necessidades de uma população em constante transformação.

Esse movimento ajuda a construir uma economia mais diversificada e preparada para acompanhar as mudanças do mercado.

Do pequeno negócio às grandes oportunidades

O crescimento empreendedor não acontece apenas nos grandes investimentos. Ele também está presente na história de comerciantes, prestadores de serviços, profissionais autônomos e pequenos empresários que decidiram transformar conhecimento e criatividade em negócios.

São iniciativas que nascem, muitas vezes, de uma necessidade ou de uma oportunidade percebida no cotidiano. Com planejamento, trabalho e capacidade de adaptação, elas passam a fazer parte da economia local e ajudam a movimentar bairros, regiões e toda a cidade.

Ao mesmo tempo, a presença de empresas maiores amplia o potencial de Uberlândia para receber investimentos, desenvolver novos mercados e conectar a economia local a outras regiões do Brasil.

Empreender também significa inovar. Em um cenário de mudanças rápidas, empresas que investem em tecnologia, novos processos e soluções diferenciadas ganham espaço e contribuem para modernizar a economia.

Uberlândia tem condições para fortalecer cada vez mais essa cultura de inovação, aproximando empresas, profissionais, instituições de ensino e iniciativas voltadas ao desenvolvimento de novos negócios.

Essa conexão cria um ambiente favorável para que ideias sejam transformadas em soluções e para que o conhecimento produzido na cidade também se converta em oportunidades.

O empreendedorismo tem impacto direto na vida das pessoas. Quando uma empresa cresce, a cadeia formada ao seu redor também pode crescer. Mais empregos significam maior circulação de renda. Mais negócios significam mais produtos e serviços. Mais investimentos podem significar novas oportunidades.

O resultado é um ciclo de desenvolvimento no qual a atividade econômica ajuda a transformar a cidade e, ao mesmo tempo, é impulsionada pelas necessidades de uma população que cresce e busca novas possibilidades.

Por isso, estimular o empreendedorismo é também investir no futuro de Uberlândia.

Cidade preparada para continuar avançando

O potencial empreendedor de Uberlândia está na capacidade de unir diferentes perfis, setores e ideias em torno de um objetivo comum: construir uma economia cada vez mais dinâmica e competitiva.

O desafio para os próximos anos é ampliar as oportunidades para quem deseja empreender, incentivar a inovação, facilitar a criação e a expansão de negócios e fortalecer as conexões entre iniciativa privada, poder público, instituições e sociedade.

Quando esses agentes trabalham de forma integrada, o crescimento deixa de ser apenas um indicador econômico e passa a ser percebido no cotidiano.

Uberlândia cresce porque existe uma rede de pessoas dispostas a fazer acontecer. São empreendedores que abrem portas, profissionais que criam soluções, empresas que investem e trabalhadores que movimentam diariamente a economia.

Esse espírito empreendedor funciona como combustível para uma cidade que busca novas oportunidades e se prepara para os desafios do futuro.

Mais negócios significam mais possibilidades. Mais inovação significa maior capacidade de adaptação. Mais empreendedorismo significa uma Uberlândia cada vez mais preparada para transformar o crescimento econômico em desenvolvimento.

Uma cidade que incentiva quem empreende também constrói caminhos para que toda a população possa avançar.

articles.title: Desfile de 7 de setembro altera dez linhas de ônibus em Natal | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudanças ocorrem das 5h às 12h desta segunda-feira (7) por causa das interdições de trânsito na região do desfile.
articles.summary: As mudanças nas linhas de ônibus em Natal ocorrem das 5h às 12h desta segunda-feira (7) devido às interdições para o desfile de 7 de setembro.
articles.body:
Ônibus passa em frente à sede da Prefeitura de Natal — Foto: Demis Roussos/STTU

Dez linhas de ônibus terão alterações temporárias nos itinerários durante o Desfile Cívico de 7 de setembro, em Natal . Segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Mobilidade Urbana (STTU), os desvios serão feitos das 5h às 12h desta segunda-feira (7), devido às interdições de trânsito na região.

As mudanças ocorrem em sentidos específicos de algumas linhas, enquanto outros trajetos permanecem sem alteração.

articles.title: 'Not charity': Nepal seeks compensation from major industrial emitters for deadly flood
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal has launched a diplomatic push to seek climate-related compensation from major greenhouse gas emitters, as the country grapples with the devasta.
articles.body: Nepal has launched a diplomatic push to seek climate-related compensation from major greenhouse gas emitters, as the country grapples with the devastating aftermath of deadly flash floods.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal said the Himalayan nation contributes "virtually negligible" greenhouse gas emissions but is bearing a disproportionate share of the consequences of climate change, including rapid glacier melt and extreme mountain disasters."We are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create. The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change," he said in an interview with Kantipur TV, excerpts of which were published by The Kathmandu Post.Khanal said Nepal was shifting its diplomatic approach from seeking "aid" to demanding "justice and compensation"."This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability," he said, adding that Nepal would raise the issue "with absolute firmness and clarity" at international forums.As per news agency PTI, the foreign minister identified the world's three largest greenhouse gas emitters and said they had a "historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.""This is a matter of civilisational survival. If our Himalayan glaciers disappear, the water security of over two billion people in South Asia dependent on rivers like the Ganges and the Trishuli will be permanently compromised. We are advocating not just for Nepal, but for the survival of South Asian civilisation," he said.Nepal has also formally approached the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, seeking urgent financial assistance following the Bhotekoshi River basin flash flood.A letter jointly signed by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Forests and Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary said the disaster had caused extensive economic and non-economic losses that exceeded Nepal's immediate response capacity.Also read: Glacier collapse at 8.37am, alert at 9.15 - Why Nepal sent disaster warning 38 minutes late'India is powerful and like God to us': What Nepal flood survivors saidMeanwhile, survivors of the August 26 flash floods have been relying on immediate humanitarian assistance, including support from neighbouring India.In Nuwakot, the Nepal-Bharat Maitri Bhawan, which houses an Ayurveda and Alternative Hospital rebuilt with financial assistance from the Embassy of India after the 2015 earthquake, has become a refuge for displaced residents.Hospital chief Dr Narendra Prasad Giri said more than 100 displaced people were staying at the facility each night, while medical teams were also being sent to nearby shelters."This building is a post-earthquake reconstruction, and it was assisted financially by the Embassy of India. This building is a core support for the people. Many devastated people who were rescued from there, we brought them here and treated, and their health is now stable," Giri told ANI.One survivor, recalling how floodwaters swept him away while he was trying to save his goats, said hospital staff reassured him after he was injured."Here, the doctors and sisters (nurses) told me, 'Don't cry, we will save you, treat your wounds, apply medicine, and make you fine right here.' They are treating me and helping me; I'm receiving good care and facilities," he said.Expressing gratitude for India's assistance, he told ANI, "Indian government is like our neighboring nation, a friend. Now that this happened in Nepal, the Indian government has given us a lot of support. India is powerful and like God to us."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nottingham attacks families not told 'stalker' had violent past
articles.summary: Nottinghamshire Police received a complaint and has referred the matter to the IOPC.
articles.body:
Families of the Nottingham attacks victims said police did not tell them a man who had taken an interest in them had a history of violence when he attempted to visit them.

Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023. He tried to kill three others.

Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, said he was told in 2025 that a man had visited his GP surgery in London. Emma Webber, Barnaby's mother, said he had also travelled to Somerset, but neither were informed of the man's history of mental ill health.

Nottinghamshire Police said it had received a complaint and referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The IOPC confirmed it had received a referral of a complaint from Nottinghamshire Police in relation to information the force allegedly withheld from the families of Calocane's victims about a potential witness who had tried to contact them.

Kumar told the BBC he was informed by Nottinghamshire Police in 2025 that a man from Nottingham, who had taken an interest in his family and the Webber family, had visited his surgery in London.

He said police gave little to no details about the man, with no mention of his past mental health history.

"They [the police officers] said it was a very lowbrow thing. There was no assessment of risk to me or my family," he added.

Kumar said it was only recently, as a result of ongoing investigations into Nottinghamshire Police, in relation to the attacks, that he was informed of further details about the man by the IOPC.

"Later, we found out from the IOPC that this guy was on the Prevent register, that he had been sectioned a few times or that he was known to be a violent offender," Kumar said.

"I'm angry. Don't place my wife, don't place my other child at risk. Do these people not realise the tragedy we've been through?

"Just be transparent. That's all we wanted."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4, Grace's mother, Dr Sinead O'Malley-Kumar, said she was "absolutely flabbergasted" that police were aware of the man's behaviour in December 2024, but did not inform families until about a year later.

"And what's more concerning is that, as victims, we weren't given the proper information," she added.

"We do not know what this man looks like. Should he ring on our doorbell? Should he come to our place of work again?

The Times reports Barnaby Webber's parents were not told for 18 months that a stalker had travelled to Somerset to try to find them.

Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, said in a social media post she was "furious".

"Now we learn that another mentally ill man with a fixation on us and the Nottingham case travelled to Somerset, including our home town, seeking out victims' families; and the police chose not to tell us," she said.

A spokesperson for the IOPC said it was "assessing the referral" from Nottinghamshire Police to decide what further action was required.

"After originally receiving information from Nottinghamshire Police we spoke to a potential witness in January 2025 in connection with our investigation concerning the force's interactions with Calocane prior to the attacks," the spokesperson added.

"It was unclear whether Calocane was the suspect for the matters that had been reported to police by the witness and the information was assessed as not relevant to our inquiries.

"We did, however, make the force aware of the information provided by the witness so it could take the appropriate safeguarding measures.

"We recognised that the families should have been updated that we'd spoken to this witness at the time and acknowledged that in a recent update to them.

A Nottinghamshire Police spokesperson said: "We received a complaint and due to the nature of the complaint referred the matter to the IOPC on August 24 and are awaiting their response.

"Unfortunately, we cannot comment any further at this stage while an investigation is underway. We have updated the complainant throughout the process."

Calocane pleaded guilty to three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and to three counts of attempted murder in November 2023.

He was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in January 2024. A public statutory inquiry, which is examining the lead-up to the attacks and decisions taken in the aftermath is set to resume in September.

What later emerged was a series of failings by authorities, including the police and mental health services - which Calocane was known to - prompting calls for a statutory public inquiry.

The Nottingham Inquiry heard from more than 100 witnesses as the lead-up to the attacks, the investigation that followed and the aftermath were examined.

articles.title: Former Hull boxer Tommy Coyle to host annual school uniform event
articles.summary: Ex-Commonwealth lightweight champion Tommy Coyle is running the event in Hull for the seventh year.
articles.body:
Free school uniforms are to be handed out in Hull by former boxer Tommy Coyle.

The ex-Commonwealth lightweight champion set up a sporting foundation when he retired from boxing in 2019 and has led a number of initiatives for underprivileged children, including a mobile boxing gym.

"If you're in a position to do good then I believe you should," he said.

The event at Coyle's gym, TC60, on Humber Street will take place on Thursday from 10:00 until 13:00 BST.

Coyle said he would be giving out unbranded uniforms of all colours and sizes with no questions asked for those who attended, working with places such as Transwaste Recycling, Cranswick and MKM.

About 400 uniforms were given to families last year, and he said it "does tend to go up year on year".

Speaking on BBC Radio Humberside , Coyle said: "It's such an expensive time of year. Everything is going up in price. Uniforms are a fortune this year.

"It's a bittersweet day – bitter in the sense that so many people need support but sweet in the sense that we can come together to support the community."

Coyle added that his reason for doing it was "a bit of a personal one".

"It goes back many years, and there was a form of bullying taking place as certain people didn't have certain makes [of clothes] at school," he said.

"I think everybody should be able to feel included at school whether they've got branded or unbranded uniform."

articles.title: Early release scheme set to free 2,500 prisoners by end of year
articles.summary: The new plan shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail.
articles.body:
About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of the year, the government's revised early prison release plan shows.

The new plan, signed into law and published online, shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail, aside from delaying the start date by a month and excluding specific offences from the programme.

Under the original plan, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months would have been eligible from 2 September to walk out of jail after serving a third of that time.

In the Commons on Wednesday, Burnham said he understood the "anguish" of victims and "listened to what they were saying".

"I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme, and we excluded rape, grooming, and child sex offences," the prime minister added.

Prisoners will now qualify for their earlier release from 1 October and officials estimate that around 700 will walk out of the prison gates that day.

From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months.

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity, with the latest Ministry of Justice figures showing the number of available spaces across the male prison estate at its lowest this year, with about 1,500 free spaces.

Under the original plan, prisons and probation services had almost six weeks to prepare this second group following the first releases, but they now have less than a fortnight.

The rest of the estimated 4,500 releases will then be phased in following the dates below. Some 1,400 more offenders were due to be released under the original plans before revisions made after certain offences were excluded.

The estimated numbers are Ministry of Justice calculations:

From 10 November, 650 offenders serving up to three years and two months

From 8 December, 550 offenders serving up to four years and three months

From 12 January 2027, 600 offenders serving up to five years and nine months

From 9 February, 500 offenders serving up to seven years and six months

From 9 March, 200 offenders serving up to nine years

From 13 April, 200 offenders serving up to 10 years

From 11 May, 250 offenders serving up to 12 years

From 9 June, 250 offenders serving more than 12 years.

The offenders serving the longer sentences, which do not become part of the scheme until next year, include more dangerous criminals who would have previously expected to spend two-thirds of their sentence behind bars.

Under the new rules this group will instead leave jail at the halfway point.

The ministerial order lists all of the 71 crimes that are exempt from the earlier release scheme, including manslaughter, rape, and sexual and grooming offences.

Prisoners on a special form of extended sentence and those on life terms are excluded from the scheme.

On Tuesday, the government explained it was creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of £110m, which is set to come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris told the BBC being released did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Norris also said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

articles.title: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night
articles.summary: Huge AI spending plans and the ongoing war in Iran are driving up borrowing costs around the world.
articles.body:
It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs.

The markets lending money to governments appear to be changing more fundamentally too.

Over summer, the message has been made clear: countries will have to pay more to borrow cash.

The immediate reason is the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, which has pushed up inflation and, in turn, raised expectations of higher interest rates in the world's major economies.

Markets had assumed tensions would subside, and so too would oil and gas prices, ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

It was wishful thinking, based on the hope that US President Donald Trump would want the conflict in the Middle East resolved well before Americans go to the polls.

But that has not happened, leaving markets pricing in higher energy prices, a chronic Gulf crisis, higher inflation for longer - and so higher interest rates.

The bigger picture is rising demand for borrowing across the world - and not just from governments. Big tech companies are turning to the same bond markets to raise hundreds of billions of dollars for investments in AI data centres.

Over $219bn (£162bn) of debt has already been issued this year by the US "hyperscalers" such as Google, Amazon and Meta, nearly a third of it in currencies other than the dollar, including sterling.

The total issued last year was $93bn, while before that it averaged less than $40bn a year. Some expect the tech giants to raise $400-$500bn from the bond markets this year. These are staggering sums, raising competition in the market and pushing up the price for governments.

Looking east, there is another major borrower: Japan.

It has the highest debt burden, relative to its GDP, of the major economies and is the biggest single lender to the US government. Until recently its central bank's interest rate was zero, but that has crept up to help combat rising inflation.

As a result, its government bond yields have been pushed to 30-year highs. The declining value of the yen complicates things, but the bottom line is that there is a change afoot in the global flow of money.

Why are UK borrowing costs rising and what does it mean for me?

The biggest factor pushing up rates is the credibility of the borrowing plans set out by major countries. The increase is not based on fears about countries "going bankrupt".

But it is based on the brutal market equation that if a country wants to borrow more, and to do so without a credible plan, especially if there are doubts over the stability of a given government, it should expect to pay a higher rate.

Influential economists lean on different factors. Mohamed el-Erian told me the AI competition in bond markets was the biggest new factor.

Lord Jim O'Neill, says the recent action has been caused by uncertainty about US policy, and in particular efforts by the US Government to try to manage down surging yields.

This brings us to the UK. The profound and rolling instability of multiple prime ministers, chancellors, policy U-turns and the seeming inability to push through major structural change in this country over the past decades, has attracted a premium.

It was part of Sir Keir Starmer's strategy to try to take on boring reforms and offer markets stability in a bid to lower borrowing costs.

It was a shock to many in the markets that despite a landslide majority, Labour could not push through plans to cut Britain's welfare bill. This added to the ups and downs in the gilt markets - the trade in British government debt.

Actually, there are signs of green shoots in the underlying economy. Economic growth has been faster than peers so far in 2026, despite the energy price spike.

Measures of consumer confidence have ticked back up again. The PM is hoping to build on these signs to help rebuild the economy.

But the ongoing rout in global bond markets raises serious questions about the coherence and detail of Burnham's broader plans.

"More public control" and more support for those struggling with the cost of living sounds like a plan for more spending, while the former could turn off potential investors looking at the country.

Burnham's former economic adviser, Lord O'Neill, told me yesterday that the PM's 10-year plan, expected in November, needs to set out how he will tackle "excessive spending".

Lord O'Neill believes showing investors he can be decisive on the state pension or the welfare bill will give him breathing room to focus on his favoured infrastructure investments.

As interest rates tick up, the trade offs facing the prime minister only get more difficult.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Manipur Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution urging the Centre to update the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in the state before conducting the census articles.title: In Yemen, dates provide lifeline for farmers with few economic options
articles.summary: Hindered by poor infrastructure and climate challenges, farmers in Yemen cling to traditional methods to harvest dates.
articles.body:
Hajr, Yemen – Under the scorching sun of eastern Yemen’s Hadramout region, locals – young and old – immerse themselves in the annual date harvest, working among dark mounds of freshly harvested fruit spread across stones.

Farmers here in Hajr, about two hours west of Hadramout’s provincial capital of Mukalla, picked the dates about a week ago from vast palm groves nearby. They then brought them to this open ground so the dates can be dried, cleaned, and eventually sold, following traditional techniques that have endured for centuries.

Nabeel Ahmed and his family arrive before sunrise and head directly to their spot on the rocky ground, where their dates are spread out.

“My wife, my brothers and I come here before sunrise and stay until the sun gets hot,” Nabeel tells Al Jazeera, as he runs his hands through a pile of dates and holds up a handful.

Farmers and their families return every day to turn and sort the dates, removing rotten or damaged fruit before preparing the harvest for sale. Their aim is to make the dates as attractive as possible to buyers.

“These rocky grounds are used to spread out the dates, clean them, and sell them to customers,” Nabeel says.

As the farmers work, buyers move between the piles, inspecting the fruit in search of good-quality dates at the lowest possible prices. Nabeel is fortunate: someone eventually agrees to buy some of his harvest.

“I harvest the dates and sell some of them, while keeping some for my family to eat. I put some into small bags for Ramadan and other days. We usually eat dates with coffee every day. This is my sole source of income,” he says, pointing to small bags filled with dates.

Beyond providing an annual source of income, dates also offer a basic food safety net for some of Hajr’s poorest families. “If a farmer cannot provide food for his children, he gives them dates and coffee, because some families cannot even afford fish and rice,” Nabeel says.

Hajr consists of scattered communities along a long valley filled with palm trees and traversed by a river. The main road connecting the district with other parts of Hadramout has deteriorated after years of poor maintenance, while roads linking its communities are largely unpaved and dusty . The district has no electricity, and mobile phone services are poor.

It has also experienced repeated outbreaks of cholera, which locals and health officials attribute mainly to inadequate sanitation and a lack of access to clean water.

Hajr might be far from Yemen’s front lines , but it is still suffering from the effects of more than a decade of war in the country, and the lack of a stable government that can alleviate poverty .

It’s why Hajr’s vast date palm groves are a lifeline here, providing income and opportunities. There are no official figures on the number of palm trees or the district’s annual date production, but local officials told Al Jazeera that there are at least 2 million palm trees in the district.

The palm trees are effectively the centre of Hajr’s economy.

At the open-air drying ground, which turns into a temporary market during the harvest season, Rashed Mohammed, a father of four, has turned down offers from several buyers at prices he considered too low.

But he worries that if he cannot sell his harvest during the few remaining days of the season, he will be unable to repay his debt to a local grocery shop.

“I owe 1 million Yemeni riyals [$640] to the grocery, and I will not be able to pay it back if I don’t sell the dates,” Rashed says.

Like many farmers in the district whose main source of income is selling dates, Rashed buys essential food for his family on credit throughout the year, promising to repay the shopkeeper after the harvest. Other farmers put off weddings, building houses or buying essential goods until they have harvested and sold their dates.

At the end of the day, if no buyers arrive, family members return home while Rashed and other farmers stay behind, sleeping in makeshift shelters built from palm fronds. They remain partly to protect their harvest from thieves and stray dogs, but also to be available around the clock in case a buyer turns up.“The customer can come at any time, so I sleep here,” Rashed says.

Farmers say one reason they continue to market their dates at the open-air market is that they cannot afford to transport their harvest to larger markets elsewhere in Yemen. Poverty is so severe, they say, that some farmers do not have enough cash to pay drivers to transport their dates and instead compensate them with plastic crates filled with dates.

Awadh Mubarak, a farmer and the head of a local farmers’ committee in Hajr’s Jawl region, says many farmers have abandoned agriculture for other jobs, including joining the security and military services, as palm trees die and date production dwindles.

Farmers say floods a few months ago destroyed a small dam that diverted water from the river to their farms, significantly reducing the amount of water reaching their palm groves and contributing to the death of trees.

The damage is visible along the road through Hajr, where numerous palms stand bare or nearly leafless, their dried fronds hanging from dead and dying trunks.

Awadh says rebuilding the dam is the farmers’ most pressing demand.

“Our primary demand is the reconstruction of the dam. The situation is extremely difficult. Many farmers have abandoned their palm groves and gone to other jobs, or emigrated,” Awadh says, showing Al Jazeera water flowing away from farmland instead of being diverted towards the groves.

Farmers have also called on investors and the government to build a date-processing and packaging factory, saying it would save them time and help them market their produce.

“We need a date-packaging factory to handle the large quantities of dates produced in the district,” Awadh says. “Instead of my family and me going out every day to clean the dates, for example, we could take them to the factory, where they could be processed in a day, saving us time and effort.”

For buyers such as Omer Mohammed, who travelled from a mountainous village in Hadramout, the reputation of Hajr’s dates and their perceived health benefits make the long journey to the district worthwhile.

“Hajr dates are the best in Hadramout because they are low in sugar,” says Omer, as he rests inside a makeshift shelter while workers pack the dates he has bought into bags.

“Back in my school days, when doctors needed blood, they would take it from residents of Hajr because they ate dates,” he says, recalling a local belief about their health benefits.

“I buy enough dates for myself and my relatives to last the entire year. If I have dates in my house, I feel food secure, even if I don’t eat them.”

Rashed Mohammed, a father-of-four, hopes to sell his dates so he can pay off his debt to his local shopkeeper [Saeed Al Batati/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Tiger Woods reaches plea deal in reckless driving case
articles.summary: Tiger Woods reached a plea deal with prosecutors Wednesday in connection with DUI charges against him following a crash near his Florida home earlier this year.
articles.body: MARTIN COUNTY, Florida — Tiger Woods reached a plea deal with prosecutors Wednesday in connection with DUI charges against him, following a car crash near his Florida home earlier this year. Woods, 50, appeared in a Martin County courtroom and pleaded no contest to a reduced charge of reckless driving and refusal to submit to a lawful test, avoiding time in prison. The troubled golfer also agreed to have his driving license suspended for five years and fined $1,500. In March, Woods was involved in a rollover on Jupiter Island, just north of Palm Beach, Florida. He initially pleaded not guilty to two charges — driving under the influence and refusing to submit to testing — in connection with the crash. Had he fought the charges and been convicted, Woods could have faced up to a year in county jail, according to prosecutors. A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt but means the accused will offer no defense. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system. Woods’ attorney declined to comment. The golf champion later left the courthouse without addressing reporters. Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl addressed reporters after the hearing. “Of all the people in the world who should not get behind the wheel of the car, it’s the gentleman who is one of the most recognizable faces on the planet,” Bakkedahl said. “Somebody will see him, whether it’s in Georgia or Nevada or New York or where have you. He’s not to drive a car.” Bakkedahl said he was unsure if the golf champion would be allowed to drive a golf cart under the terms of the deal. Woods arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law. She sat behind him during the hearing. The March crash involved a dark Land Rover that Woods had been driving and a truck carrying a trailer, according to officials. At the time, the driver of the truck said he was starting to turn into a driveway off a two-lane road when he looked into his mirror and saw Woods driving “at high speeds.” The driver tried veering off the road, but Woods’ Land Rover “overtook” the truck at the last minute, swerving to avoid a crash, officials said. Woods ultimately clipped the back of the trailer. Woods’ SUV rolled onto the driver’s side door, according to officials, leaving the golfer to exit by climbing out of the window. Neither Woods nor the truck driver was injured in the crash. Woods told authorities that he was under the influence and had two hydrocodone pills in his pocket upon his arrest, Bakkedahl said. In the days following the incident, Woods said in a statement on social media that he was seeking treatment. “I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in,” he wrote. Bakkedahl described Woods and his attorney as being cooperative in handing over evidence to officials. Several days before the crash, Woods played in a match in the finals for Tomorrow’s Golf League. His team, Jupiter Links Golf Club, lost to the Los Angeles Golf Club in the competition. Woods, who is among the most influential figures in golf, has been involved in several road incidents in recent years. In 2021, he was involved in a rollover in Southern California but did not face criminal charges. The golf champion was also arrested and charged with a DUI in Florida in 2017. He checked himself into a clinic that same year.

articles.title: EU or Eurasia: Why Putin sparred with Armenia’s PM
articles.summary: Relations between Russia and Armenia have reached historic lows as Yerevan pivots towards the West.
articles.body:
Russia President Vladimir Putin has warned Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan that Yerevan’s bid to join the European Union could disrupt trade with Moscow.

Relations between the two countries have reached historic lows as Yerevan pivots towards the West, prompting sharp economic and political retaliation from Moscow.

In a tense meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital on Tuesday, Putin said that Moscow needs clarity on whether Yerevan wants to join the EU so it can decide on the future of bilateral trade with Armenia.

Putin also said that Armenia joining the EU would be tantamount to declaring a break from the Eurasian Economic Union (EEU) – a Russia-led grouping of several post-Soviet states.

Last April, Yerevan decided to adopt a law to launch the process of EU accession – a sticking point for Russia, which views its neighbouring post-Soviet countries as a vital security shield between its borders and the European Union.

In Bishkek, Armenia’s Pashinyan stressed that Yerevan has not violated any of its obligations towards Russia through its EU accession process and did not want to leave the EEU.

What happened at the meeting? Here’s what we know:

At their meeting on Tuesday, according to the Kremlin, Putin told Pashinyan that while Russia is a key economic and trade partner to Armenia, Yerevan’s EU aspirations could create complications for its EEU membership.

“Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU is the natural and legitimate right of the country and its people. Armenia is a sovereign state, and it is for the Armenian people to determine the trajectory of their own development,” Putin said.

“Nevertheless, this unquestionably creates complications for Armenia’s continued membership in the Eurasian Economic Union, and threatens to erode the advantages the Republic enjoys on the EEU market and to sever established trade links,” he added.

Pashinyan, however, said Armenia’s decision last year to adopt a law launching the process of EU accession did not violate its obligations to Russia or the EEU and that it was only an alternative his government had given to the people of Armenia.

What are Armenia and Russia’s relations like?

After the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, Armenia became Russia’s closest ally in the South Caucasus, with the two nations developing their trade, economic and political ties. Armenia has also long been Russia’s closest regional ally, a Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) member, host to a Russian military base and is dependent on Russian gas.

Currently, Russia is Armenia’s key trade and economic partner, accounting for roughly 30 percent of its trade, and an investor in Armenia’s economy. In the first half of this year, bilateral trade also reached $2.5bn.

But despite economic ties, relations between the two countries have been tense since 2023, after the historical conflict in the Nagorno-Karabakh region of Azerbaijan erupted again.

Russia, which is fighting its own war in Ukraine, did not intervene militarily when Azerbaijan launched a major military offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh, which had a large Armenian population and had been de facto independent since the 1990s.

Laurentiu Plesca, a political analyst and researcher focusing on EU enlargement and European security at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Al Jazeera that Moscow decision not to support Yerevan during the Karabakh war in 2023 led to Armenia’s pivot towards the West.

He said that this, in turn, upset Moscow, further souring relations.

“Russia started blocking imports of Armenian goods and is threatening to suspend the duty-free supply of gas, oil products, and diamonds to Armenia,” he said.

“The EU, in turn, has pledged economic support to offset that pressure,” he added.

In early July, the European Commission’s President Ursula von der Leyen also told Yerevan that it could count on the EU amid any economic pressure from Russia and pledged an additional 18 million euros (about $20m) as ⁠part of a broader 52 million euros (about $60m) economic support package.

Last April, Armenia’s president signed into law a bill that set the legal foundation for the country to move towards joining the EU.

Pashinyan, who took power in 2018 and was part of launching the EU bid, has repeatedly stressed that the bill did not represent an application to join the EU, but the start of a broader process of integration.

However, in July this year, Pashinyan told lawmakers in the country that Armenia would decide its future EU membership by holding a referendum “in the near future”.

Yerevan has significantly deepened its European ties, hosting its first official EU summit last month alongside a wider European gathering attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Armenia also hosted French President Emmanuel Macron for a high-profile state visit, which provoked sharp criticism from the Kremlin after a video emerged of Macron singing while Pashinyan played the drums.

Putin has previously warned Armenia that it views membership in the EU as incompatible with the EEU, and Armenia would have to leave if it joins the EU.

The EEU is a group of former Soviet Union countries that coordinate economic and trade policies. Its members are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. The group’s treaty was established in May 2014, and it began its operations in January 2015.

According to a 2022 Chatham House report, the EEU is in effect a Russian-led effort to create a Eurasian counterpart to the EU.

So why is Armenia’s EU bid a point of tension for Russia and the EEU?

According to the Chatham House report, the EEU serves an important geopolitical purpose for Russia.

“Putin sees it as part of his drive to re-establish the Russian sphere of influence lost by the dissolution of the Soviet Union,” the report’s writers emphasised.

That’s why Armenia seeking closer ties with the EU represents an attempt to break from Russia’s dominance of its neighbourhood, in the eyes of the Kremlin.

In June, Pashinyan rejected a call from Moscow to hold an immediate referendum on leaving the EEU to join the European Union.

Tensions had boiled over at the EEU summit in Kazakhstan on May 29, as Putin and fellow bloc members Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement urging Armenia to hold the referendum “as soon as possible”.

Putin also appeared to make a barely veiled threat at the EEU summit, warning Armenia against pursuing its Western ambitions, and referring to Russia’s war in Ukraine, said that the “Ukrainian scenario” had also begun with Kyiv’s EU aspirations.

In a video address broadcast on social media, Pashinyan had responded to Putin and stated that his government would continue working within the EEU until a choice between the two blocs “becomes unavoidable”, noting that any referendum before Armenia formally applies for EU candidate status remains purely theoretical.

“Putting a theoretical choice to a referendum is, of course, neither very sensible nor justified,” Pashinyan had said.

At the SCO summit, however, he reiterated that Yerevan had no plans to leave the EEU and said that Moscow has always supported the development of friendly and mutually beneficial relations with Yerevan.

Plesca, the political analyst, said that at its core, there is a tug-of-war over Armenia’s strategic alignment, playing out on two fronts.

“But the pro-EU stance is already clear, and Moscow wants to reverse it. Having failed to do so at the ballot box in the recent parliamentary elections in June, it is now compensating with economic blackmail,” he said. During Armenia’s parliamentary elections in June, Moscow was accused of seeking to tip the scales by exerting economic and diplomatic pressure on Pashinyan’s government.

He noted that while Armenia does have the legal right to join the EU, doing so while still inside the EEU customs union would be legally ambiguous.

“There’s no mechanism to expel a member, and Armenia hasn’t triggered the six-month exit notice, so an EU bid doesn’t automatically breach” its obligations towards the EEU, Plesca said. “That’s exactly the trap Yerevan is navigating, keeping a foot in both camps for now, while Moscow insists that’s not possible.”

He added that for Russia, Armenia’s EU bid is also more about losing a foothold in the South Caucasus region.

articles.title: Pak pleads for dialogue after India stands firm on suspending Indus Water Treaty
articles.summary: Pakistan News: NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan on Wednesday urged New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement.According to news agency PTI, Pakistan foreign office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said the Permanent Court of Arbitration had reaffirmed that the treaty remained fully enforced and binding. Pakistan, he said, would take “all possible measures” to ensure the decision was implemented.Andrabi said Pakistan remained committed to implementing the treaty in letter and spirit in accordance with its language and provisions.Pakistan will continue to urge India to reciprocate with the same approach whereby the treaty is upheld in letter and spirit and in its full legal documented provisions, he said, according to PTI.Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty after India placed it in abeyance.India rejects tribunal rulingIndia, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.On Monday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, “India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”“India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force,” the ministry said.MEA said the Court of Arbitration had issued what it termed an award on May 15, 2026, concerning maximum pondage supplemental to an earlier award on issues of general interpretation of the IWT."This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body", the ministry stated.India has maintained that the establishment of the arbitral body itself violates the IWT and that it has no jurisdiction over India’s sovereign decision to place the treaty in abeyance.Water, terrorism and the SCOThe dispute also featured indirectly at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, in Bishkek, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for action against countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy.“We cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach,” Modi said, calling for the dismantling of terrorist ecosystems, including funding networks, recruitment pipelines and territorial sanctuaries.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking at the summit, described water as the region’s “lifeblood” and said it “must never be weaponised”.“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit,” Sharif said, according to Dawn.India placed the IWT in abeyance following the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. The Cabinet Committee on Security took the decision on April 23, 2025, with New Delhi saying the conditions underlying the treaty had fundamentally changed.India has said the treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism”.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: CNN founder Ted Turner’s New Mexico ranch helped save North America’s rarest large tortoise, growing its population from 30 to about 800
articles.summary: US News: For thousands of years, the Bolson tortoise had been missing from the grasslands of New Mexico. Then a private ranch offered the species something it .
articles.body: For thousands of years, the Bolson tortoise had been missing from the grasslands of New Mexico. Then a private ranch offered the species something it had not had in generations: space to start again. What began with just 30 captive tortoises grew into a population of roughly 800 through a long-running conservation effort backed by Ted Turner’s Turner Endangered Species Fund. Among the animals was Gertie, an elderly female estimated to be at least 80 years old, whose eggs have helped keep the breeding programme going.As reported by Turtle Conservancy, in 2023, nearly two dozen tortoises were released onto Turner’s vast Armendaris Ranch, marking a new chapter in the attempt to establish a free-living population. Their return is not a quick rescue story. It is a slow experiment in whether a species absent from the American Southwest for thousands of years can find its way home again.How Ted Turner helped bring the Bolson tortoise back to the USThe Bolson tortoise is North America’s largest and rarest tortoise species. It was not even known to science until the late 1950s, and much about its natural history remains poorly understood. Fossil evidence, however, shows that its range was once far wider than it is today.The tortoise once occupied parts of the southwestern United States and extended into the southern Great Plains, including areas of what are now Texas and Oklahoma. In New Mexico, its disappearance dates back thousands of years.Its remaining wild population is now concentrated in the grasslands of north-central Mexico. Fewer than 2,500 animals are thought to survive there, and the population continues to face pressure from people collecting tortoises as pets, hunting them for food and converting grassland habitat to farmland.Ted Turner’s conservation effort began with just 30 Bolson tortoisesPart of the answer began decades ago with a group of captive Bolson tortoises kept at the Appleton-Whittell Research Ranch.Among them was a large female named Gertie. Her exact age is unknown, although biologists estimate that she is at least in her 80s. Despite her age, she remains of breeding age and has continued producing eggs.According to the US Fish & Wildlife Service, when caretaker Ariel Appleton died in 2004, her estate donated the tortoises to facilities belonging to Ted Turner’s Turner Endangered Species Fund in southern New Mexico. Biologists Scott Hillard and Chris Wiese subsequently began working to build a recovery population that could eventually support reintroduction.There were only 30 tortoises in the Appleton group; that number would eventually become 800.More than 400 hatchlings helped Ted Turner build a future for the speciesThe Turner project has operated on a timetable very different from that of most conservation programmes. Bolson tortoises are slow-growing animals, and raising young to adulthood takes years.According to Tucson Herpetological Society and AP News, since 2006, work at the Turner ranch and the Living Desert Zoo and Gardens in Carlsbad has produced more than 400 hatchlings. Over time, the captive population assembled by the Turner Endangered Species Fund and its partners reached roughly 800 tortoises.For the biologists involved, simply increasing the number of animals was never the final objective. The intention was to produce tortoises capable of living without the constant protection of captivity.A new home on a vast New Mexico ranchThe Armendaris Ranch in central New Mexico covers more than 560 square miles, or about 1,450 square kilometres. Its grassland landscape resembles the kind of habitat where Bolson tortoises live in Mexico, making it a candidate for the next stage of the project.In September 2023, nearly two dozen tortoises were released there, including 20 adults. They were initially placed in a 16.5-acre enclosure where they could move around without the protection of conventional captive facilities.The animals were fitted with transponders so wildlife managers could keep track of them. Monitoring is expected to be limited, with checks once a year rather than constant intervention.The intention is eventually to let them expand beyond the enclosure and establish a free-ranging population across suitable parts of the ranch. For the tortoises, that means burrows, grass, weather and predators rather than keepers and pens.Deep burrows protect the Bolson tortoise but can also expose it to peopleA Bolson tortoise is not an animal that spends its days wandering across open ground.The species spends roughly 85% of its time in earthen burrows, some of which can reach around 20 metres in length. The burrows provide shelter from the harsh conditions of the grasslands and form an important part of the animal's daily life.When they sense movement, they can head towards the entrance of their burrow to investigate or defend it. The same instinct can expose them to people, particularly in areas where tortoises are collected.The Turner ranch offers something the remaining wild population increasingly lacks: a large, remote landscape where human contact can be kept to a minimum.The 2023 agreement changed what recovery could look likeThe Bolson tortoise had traditionally been treated under US wildlife policy as a foreign endangered species. Since the species had disappeared from the United States thousands of years ago, conservationists had to consider whether the Endangered Species Act could be used to support its recovery within the country.That question became less theoretical in September 2023, when the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the Turner organisation entered into a Safe Harbor Agreement.The agreement cleared the way for captive tortoises to be released on the ranch and helped create a framework for establishing a free-living population. It also gave private landowners protections from certain additional regulatory burdens associated with endangered species recovery.The arrangement could eventually help officials explore similar approaches for other species whose recovery depends on private land.Recovery may take longer than a human lifetimeThe biggest challenge may simply be time. A hatchling can take several years or more to reach just over 11 centimetres in length, depending on weather and the availability of food. Adults can eventually reach about 37 centimetres.US Fish and Wildlife Service field supervisor Shawn Sartorius has said the results of the breeding and restoration work may not be known during his lifetime. The population being established now is intended to be something that can pass to the next generation of conservationists.Gertie offers an unusual link between those generations. The elderly tortoise helped anchor the original captive population and is still producing offspring.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Palestinians in fear as Israeli forces mount pogroms on West Bank mosques
articles.summary: Palestinian witnesses recount the coordinated Israeli army and settler attacks on mosques in the occupied West Bank.
articles.body:
Naim Ahmed Faraj, along with dozens of worshippers, was standing for the evening (Isha) prayers, when Israeli forces threw tear gas canisters inside their mosque in Madama village near Nablus. Faraj, 66, who suffers from joint and heart ailments, collapsed due to suffocation.

Faraj’s son, Mohammed Naim, says his father fell semiconscious and his condition deteriorated after inhaling tear gas. The 66-year-old regained consciousness gradually after he was rushed home inside a car as there were no ambulances available, according to Naim.

“The mosque is supposed to be a safe haven where people can pray without being attacked. But lately – and for a long time now – the mosque has become a source of anxiety,” Naim told Al Jazeera, adding that worshippers now fear while going to mosques for prayers amid escalating violence in the occupied West Bank.

The Madama attack is part of a sharply rising wave of Israeli settler and military pogroms across the occupied territory, which Palestinian sources say are emboldened by extremist government ministers like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Naim described these raids as daily occurrences, deliberately timed during prayer hours to maximise panic. He noted that soldiers and settlers regularly collaborate to “terrorise” the local population.

“Our village has become like an island surrounded from all sides by settlements, the bypass road, and the army, and we do not have any outlet or area we can go to,” Naim said, pointing out the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, which cut through Palestinian towns and villages.

More than 750,000 settlers live in illegal settlements throughout the occupied Palestinian territory, and their numbers continue to rise as top Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, publicly oppose the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state.

The anti-Palestinian rhetoric and physical attacks have particularly exploded in recent weeks as Israeli politicians campaign for next month’s general elections. Last week, far-right Israeli Knesset member Zvi Sukkot stormed Madama village and smashed a Palestinian memorial with a sledgehammer.

Hours after the attack in Madama, Israeli settlers launched a separate violent raid on the Imad al-Din Zanki mosque in the nearby town of Bazariya in the occupied West Bank.

Attackers poured flammable liquids onto the ground floor of the building and ignited it.

Taysir Safarini, the former head of the Bazariya village council, recounted the frantic response.

“Neighbours woke up, of course, to the burning flames, and informed the civil defence crews in Anabta, and tried to extinguish the fire themselves to stop [it] from spreading,” Safarini told Al Jazeera.

The settlers also sprayed Hebrew graffiti on the walls, including threats to kill Arabs and a mocking message directed at the United States ambassador to Israel reading: “Huckabee, greetings from the terrorists.”

Mike Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has voiced support for Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, recently called the settlers “ terrorists “.

Following the attacks, the office of Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas warned that such violations risk triggering a catastrophic religious war.

The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Affairs condemned the continued pogroms, describing the targeting of mosques as a flagrant violation of international law.

The ministry documented that at least 13 mosques have been vandalised or burned by Israeli settlers and forces since the start of the year.

This targeting extends far beyond rural villages; in a detailed August report, the ministry recorded 26 incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound and 155 instances in which the call to prayer was banned at the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron.

The human toll of these pogroms is high.

According to the United Nations, at least 76 Palestinians, including 18 children, have been killed in the territory this year, and some 3,800 people have been displaced.

The UN recorded more than 1,450 settler attacks resulting in roughly 1,040 injuries, while the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission estimates the total number of attacks exceeds 6,000.

For Palestinian residents, the relentless violence has shattered any semblance of safety, forcing families to make choices about their basic movements.

“For example, I do not allow my son to go to the mosque or anywhere else out of fear for him, and I keep him at home and tell him do not go out in these times due to the daily incursions,” Naim told Al Jazeera.
